title: Least Squares, Projections & Conditioning
summary: Least squares as an orthogonal projection, the normal equations and why they square the condition number, and how Householder QR solves the same problem stably.
takeaways: The least-squares fit projects b onto the column space of A, so the residual is orthogonal to every column.
An orthogonal projector is symmetric and idempotent (P² = P), and its trace equals the rank.
The condition number σ_max/σ_min estimates the digits you lose. Forming AᵀA squares it.
Householder QR solves Rx = Qᵀb without squaring κ. Choose the reflection sign opposite to x[0] to avoid cancellation.

steps.label: Reflect
steps.detail: For each column k, a reflection I − 2vvᵀ zeroes everything below the diagonal.

steps.label: Accumulate
steps.detail: The reflected matrix is R. Applying the reflectors to the identity gives Q.

steps.label: Rotate b
steps.detail: Compute Qᵀb; Q preserves lengths, so the problem becomes Rx ≈ Qᵀb.

steps.label: Back-substitute
steps.detail: Solve the triangular system from the last row up.

steps.label: Check
steps.detail: The residual b − Ax must be orthogonal to the columns: Aᵀ(b − Ax) ≈ 0.

terms.definition: AᵀA x = Aᵀb, the condition that the residual is orthogonal to the column space.
P = A(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ = QQᵀ, which maps any vector to its closest point in the column space.
κ(A) = σ_max / σ_min, the worst-case amplification of relative input error.
H = I − 2vvᵀ with ‖v‖ = 1: an orthogonal matrix that mirrors vectors across the plane perpendicular to v.
Subtracting two nearly equal floating-point numbers, which leaves only rounding noise in the result.
